{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Robert Hilton Meservey''' (April 1, 1921, in [[Hanover, New Hampshire]] – June 18, 2013, in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]])<ref name=AIP>{{cite web|title=Robert Meservey|website=American Institute of Physics|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11606037.html}}</ref> was an American physicist, specializing in [[condensed matter physics]]. He is known as the co-discoverer, with {{ill|Paul Tedrow|de}}, of spin-polarized tunneling,<ref name=obitPhysicsToday>{{cite journal|author=Moodera, Jagadeesh S.|author2=Tedrow, Paul M.|title=Obituary. Robert Meservey|journal=Physics Today|date=28 October 2013|doi=10.1063/PT.5.6007|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/PT.5.6007/full/|url-access=subscription}}</ref> which enabled the development of [[spin polarized scanning tunneling microscopy]] and other applications.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Meservey, R.|author2=Tedrow, P. M.|title=Spin-polarized electron tunneling|journal=Physics Reports|volume=238|issue=4|pages=173–243|date=March 1994|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(94)90105-8|bibcode=1994PhR...238..173M}} (over 1500 citations)</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Alam, Kazi M.|author2=Pramanik, Sandipan|title=Spin transport in organic semiconductors: A brief overview of the first eight years|year=2010|class=cond-mat.mes-hall|eprint=1005.1118}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Robert H. Meservey matriculated in 1939 at [[Dartmouth College]], where he was a varsity athlete.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert H. Meservey|website= Wearers of the Green, Official Site of Dartmouth College Varsity Athletics|url=https://dartmouthsports.com/honors/wearers-of-the-green/robert-h-meservey/1980}}</ref> He joined the U.S. Army on April 6, 1943, but graduated from Dartmouth before going on active duty slightly later.

After his discharge from the U.S. Army, he worked for several years as a highly successful, independent professorial photographer. He photographed several famous people, including [[Robert Frost]], [[John F. Kennedy]] (JFK), and [[Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis|Jacqueline Bouvier]], who married JFK in 1953. Meservey's best-known photograph is of Jacqueline Bouvier, descending the stairs at her [[Debutant|debutant party]] in the summer of 1947. When JFK became the U.S. President, the photograph appeared on several magazine covers and also appeared in many later books.<ref name=obitMIT>{{cite web|title=Robert Meservey, pioneering MIT physicist, dies at 92|website=MIT News, Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=July 1, 2013|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2013/obit-meservey-physics.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1953 – Ann Lowe, Jacqueline Kennedy's Wedding Dress|website=Fashion History Timeline (fashion history.fitny.edu/1953)|url=https://fashionhistory.fitnyc.edu/1953-lowe-kennedy-wedding-dress/}} (See Figure 12.)</ref> Meservey other work included a series of photographs of Dartmouth College and fashion and architectural photography in New York City and [[Newport, Rhode Island]]. Several of his photographs were published in [[Antoinette Downing]] and [[Vincent Scully]]'s prize-winning 1952 book ''Architectural Heritage of Newport Rhode Island: 1640–1915'', published by Harvard University Press.<ref name=obitMIT/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Egbert, Donald Drew|author-link=Donald Drew Egbert|year=1953|title=Review of ''The Architectural Heritage of Newport, Rhode Island, 1640–1915'' by Antoinette F. Downing and Vincent J. Scully, Jr.|journal=The Art Bulletin|volume=35|issue=4|pages=326–328|doi=10.1080/00043079.1953.11408502}}</ref> Downing and Scully's book contains reproductions of Meservey's photographs of [[Goddard and Townsend|Newport's historic Christopher Townsend House and Job Townsend House]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Downing, Antoinette Forrester|author2=Scully Jr., Vincent|title=Architectural Heritage of Newport Rhode Island: 1640–1915|year=1967|publisher=C. N. Potter|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WrJWAAAAMAAJ&q=meservey}} (reprint of 1952 book) After 1952, the Job Townsend House was demolished.</ref>

From 1951 to 1955 Meservey was employed as a physicist at the U.S. Army's ERDL.<ref name=AIP/> There he worked on the development, during the [[Korean War]], of night vision equipment and also did graduate study in physics and mathematics at [[George Washington University]]. One of his physics professors was [[George Gamow]].<ref name=obitMIT/> In 1955 Meservey became a graduate student at [[Yale University]], where he worked in the low temperature physics group directed by Cecil Taverner Lane (1904–1991).<ref name=obitMIT/> Meservey continued his work on night vision equipment from 1955 to 1960 as a consultant for the [[Perkin Elmer Corporation]], during his graduate study at [[Yale University]].<ref name=AIP/> With Lane as his thesis advisor, he received in 1961 his Ph.D with thesis entitled ''An Optical Study of the Dynamics of Liquid Helium''.<ref>{{cite book|author=Meservey, Robert Hilton|title=An Optical Study of the Dynamics of Liquid Helium|publisher=Yale University|bibcode=1961PhDT........14M}}</ref>

He worked from 1961 to 1963 at [[MIT Lincoln Laboratory]].<ref name=AIP/> There he co-authored, with [[David Douglass (physicist)|David Douglass]], an important paper on superconducting tunneling.<ref name=obitMIT/><ref>{{cite book|editor=Davies, Roy Osborne|chapter=''Measurements of the Superconducting Energy Gap in Lead and Aluminium Films'' by D. H. Douglass Jr. and R. H. Meservery|title=Proceedings of the Eighth International Conference on Low Temperature Physics|volume=8|page=180|year=1963|publisher=[[Butterworths]]|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Auk6PwAACAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Energy Gap Measurements by Tunneling Between Superconducting Films. I. Temperature Dependence|author=Douglass, D. H.|author2=Meservey, R.|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume =135|issue=1A|pages=A19–A23|date=July 1964|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.135.A19|bibcode=1964PhRv..135...19D}}</ref> Meservey was a senior scientist at MIT's [[Francis Bitter Magnet Laboratory]] from 1963 to 1994, when he retired.<ref name=obitPhysicsToday/> His doctoral students include [[Jagadeesh Moodera]] and Paul Tedrow.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert Hilton Meservey|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=634854}}</ref>

In 1995, Meservey, with Jagadeesh Moodera and other team members, discovered large magneto-resistance occurring at room temperature in ferromagnetic-ferromagnetic tunnel junctions. This breakthrough enabled the development of a new generation of "computers with extreme high density drives and nonvolatile magnetic memory/logic devices."<ref name=obitPhysicsToday/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Moodera, Jagadeesh Subbaiah|author2=Kinder, Lisa R.|author3=Wong, Terrilyn M.|author4=Meservey, R.|title=Large magnetoresistance at room temperature in ferromagnetic thin film tunnel junctions|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=74|issue=16|year=1995|pages=3273–3276|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.3273|pmid=10058155|bibcode=1995PhRvL..74.3273M}} (over 4650 citations)</ref>

Meservey was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name=obitPhysicsToday/> In 2009 he received, jointly with {{ill|Terunobu Miyazaki|de}}, Jagadeesh Moodera, and Paul Tedrow, the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] for their "pioneering work in the field of spin-dependent tunneling and for the application of these phenomena to the field of [[magnetoelectronics]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Meservey&first_nm=Robert&year=2009|title=2009 Oliver E. Buckley Prize Condensed Matter Physics Prize Recipient, Robert Meservey|website=American Physical Society}}</ref>

==Family==
Robert was the younger son of Arthur Bond Meservey (1885–1952), who was the chair of Dartmouth College's department of physics, and Anne White Meservey (1886–1970). Robert H. Meservey had a sister, Ellen, and a brother, Edward.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Prof. Meservey Dies|magazine=Dartmouth Alumni Magazine|date=June 1952|page=28|url=https://archive.dartmouthalumnimagazine.com/article/1952/6/1/prof-meservey-dies}}</ref> Edward B. Meservey (1916–2009) also became a Dartmouth alumnus, a ski champion,<ref>{{cite web|title=Edward B. Meservey|website=Wearers of the Green, Official Site of Dartmouth College Varsity Athletics|url=https://dartmouthsports.com/honors/wearers-of-the-green/edward-b-meservey/1975}}</ref> and a physicist.<ref>{{cite web|title=First Woman Graduate Student|website=Princeton University (princeton.edu/frist/iconography) page 44|url=https://www.princeton.edu/frist/iconography/p44.shtml}}</ref> Edward's wife, Sabra Follett Meservey (1924–1994), was the first woman to formally enroll as a graduate student for a higher degree at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Chosen: The Hidden History of Admission and Exclusion at Harvard, Yale, and Princeton|author=Karabel, Jerome|author-link=Jerome Karabel|year=2005
|page=427|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=9780618773558|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zwf-Ofc--toC&pg=PA427}}</ref> The couple met in Istanbul, where they both taught at a girls' school.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Princeton Alumni Weekly|volume=63|date=February 18, 1964|page=5|title=Mrs. Meservey, M.A., University News|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ohRbAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA17-PA5}}</ref> (She was [[Barbara Newhall Follett]]'s sister.)<ref>{{cite web|title=Photos of Barbara's Family|website=Farksolia, Barbara Newhall Follett's life and letters (farksolia.org)|url=https://farksolia.org/barbaras-family-a-few-photographs/}}</ref>

On September 29, 1953, in Arlington, Virginia, Robert H. Meservey married Evelyn Bradford Miller (1931–2014). Upon his death he was survived by his widow, their two married daughters, and four grandchildren.<ref name=obitMIT/>
